concepts.name: Dual Control System: Structure and Power Sharing
key_dimensions: Relationship between the newly created Board of Control and the Court of Directors of East India Company
Which body held supremacy in civil, military, and revenue matters vs. commercial matters
Why it was called 'dual' and how it differed from the earlier single-authority model under Regulating Act 1773
UPSC trap: Common confusion between Board of Control having 'superintendence' vs. full ownership of Indian administration

concepts.name: Board of Control: Composition and Authority
key_dimensions: Exact composition — 6 members including Secretary of State, Chancellor of the Exchequer, and 4 Privy Councillors appointed by the Crown
Power to superintend, direct, and control all civil, military, and revenue affairs in India
Authority to send secret dispatches to India without informing the Court of Directors — a critical trap point
Distinction between Board of Control (government body) vs. Court of Directors (Company body) — overlapping jurisdiction traps

concepts.name: Court of Directors: Retained Powers and Limitations
key_dimensions: Court of Directors retained control over commercial/trade functions of the Company
Lost effective control over political, military, and revenue affairs to the Board of Control
Secret Committee of three Directors created — bypassing the full Court for urgent/secret dispatches
UPSC trap: Directors could still nominate Indian appointments but Crown/Board held veto power

concepts.name: Secret Committee of the Court of Directors
key_dimensions: Composition: Three senior Directors forming the Secret Committee
Purpose: To transmit secret and urgent orders to India without full Court knowledge
Functioned under the direction of the Board of Control, undermining Director autonomy
Significance: First institutionalized secrecy mechanism in Indian colonial administration

concepts.name: Governor-General: Empowerment and Council Dynamics
key_dimensions: Council size reduced from four members (Regulating Act) to three members — Governor-General now had a casting vote advantage
Governor-General given overriding powers over the Council in matters of urgency — strengthening executive authority
Comparison with Regulating Act 1773 where Council frequently overruled the Governor-General (e.g., Hastings vs. Council)
UPSC trap: Governor-General could override Council but NOT act entirely alone — checks still existed

concepts.name: Subordination of Bombay and Madras Presidencies
key_dimensions: Pitt's Act explicitly made Bombay and Madras Presidencies subordinate to Bengal Presidency (Governor-General in Council)
Earlier Regulating Act 1773 had attempted this but was vague and ineffective in practice
Presidencies could act independently only in cases of 'imminent necessity' — a critical exception
Significance: Laid foundation for centralized imperial administration under Bengal

concepts.name: Prohibition on Wars and Treaties of Aggression
key_dimensions: Act explicitly prohibited the Company from entering into wars of aggression or treaties of aggression in India
Described wars of conquest as 'repugnant to the wish, the honour, and the policy of this nation'
UPSC trap: Prohibition applied to offensive wars — defensive wars and subsidiary alliances found legal gray areas
Practical contradiction: British expansion continued despite this clause — significance for policy vs. practice questions

concepts.name: India Declared a 'British Possession': Sovereignty Implications
key_dimensions: Pitt's Act was the first legislation to use the term 'the territorial possessions of the Crown in India'
Marked the formal acknowledgment that Indian territories were British possessions, not merely Company trade zones
Contrast with pre-1784 position where Company acted as a trading entity, not a sovereign power
Constitutional significance: Bridged Company rule and eventual Crown rule (1858)

concepts.name: Pitt's India Act vs. Regulating Act 1773: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Regulating Act: First attempt at parliamentary oversight but gave no direct control to Crown; Pitt's Act gave direct Crown control via Board
Regulating Act created a 4-member Council that could outvote the Governor-General; Pitt's Act reduced it to 3 and strengthened Governor-General
Regulating Act had no mechanism to override Court of Directors; Pitt's Act created Board of Control with supremacy
UPSC trap: Both acts left the Company in existence — neither abolished the Company; full Crown takeover only in 1858

concepts.name: Amending Acts of 1786: Extension of Pitt's Act Powers
key_dimensions: Act of 1786 further empowered the Governor-General — allowed him to override Council in specified circumstances
Specifically enabled Cornwallis to accept the Governor-Generalship by granting him Commander-in-Chief powers simultaneously
UPSC trap: Often misattributed — the 1786 amendment is an extension of Pitt's Act, not a standalone legislation
Shows that Pitt's Act itself was considered incomplete and required immediate supplementation

concepts.name: Failure of Fox's India Bill 1783 as the Immediate Precursor
key_dimensions: Fox's Bill proposed transferring Company patronage to 7 Crown-appointed Commissioners — seen as politicizing Indian revenues
Rejected by House of Lords after George III signaled opposition — led to fall of Fox-North Coalition
Pitt's Act was a deliberate moderate alternative — kept Company's commercial functions intact to avoid Fox's controversy
UPSC trap: Fox's Bill failed politically, not on constitutional merits — understanding this distinction is key

concepts.name: Parliamentary Sovereignty vs. Company Charter: Constitutional Tension
key_dimensions: Company operated under royal charters (1600, 1661, 1683, 1726) — Pitt's Act represented Parliament overriding chartered rights
Established the principle that parliamentary legislation could modify Company's chartered privileges
Tension between property rights of shareholders and public interest in governing India
Precedent for future parliamentary interventions: Charter Acts of 1813, 1833, 1853, and Government of India Act 1858

concepts.name: Accountability Mechanisms: Prevention of Corruption
key_dimensions: Act introduced stricter provisions against Company servants accepting gifts, bribes, or presents from Indian rulers
Connected to the broader context of Warren Hastings' impeachment (1787) — act pre-empted such controversies
Company servants returning to England with Indian wealth ('Nabobs') had become a political scandal
UPSC trap: Provisions were stronger on paper than in practice — enforcement remained with the Company itself

concepts.name: Governor-General's Position in the Imperial Hierarchy Post-1784
key_dimensions: Post-Pitt's Act, Governor-General became the pivot between Board of Control (London) and Indian administration
Answered to both the Board of Control AND the Court of Directors — creating dual accountability
Power to override Bombay and Madras Governors made him the de facto viceroy before the title was formalized
UPSC trap: Governor-General was NOT appointed by Parliament — still appointed by Court of Directors with Crown approval

concepts.name: Commercial vs. Political Functions: The Fundamental Division
key_dimensions: Pitt's Act made a conceptual distinction: Company retained commercial monopoly; Crown controlled political/territorial affairs
This division was inherently contradictory as political power and trade were inseparable in Indian context
Charter Act of 1813 ended trade monopoly — removing the commercial rationale for Company's continued existence
UPSC trap: Even after 1784, Company remained an intermediary — direct Crown rule came only in 1858, not 1784

concepts.name: Impact on Indian Rulers and Non-Interference Principle
key_dimensions: Prohibition on offensive wars implied a 'non-interference' doctrine with Indian states — violated almost immediately
Subsidiary Alliance System (Wellesley, post-1798) technically adhered to the letter but violated the spirit of the Act
How Pitt's Act paradoxically enabled expansion by requiring 'defense' justifications for wars
UPSC trap: Non-interference was a declared principle, not a practiced policy — examiners test this gap

concepts.name: Long-term Constitutional Legacy: Bridge to Crown Rule
key_dimensions: Pitt's Act established the template of parliamentary oversight that evolved through Charter Acts into direct Crown rule
Board of Control (1784) → President of Board of Control became de facto 'Minister for India' → Secretary of State for India (1858)
First time Crown (through ministers accountable to Parliament) held formal supervisory power over Indian administration
Significance for UPSC: Understanding 1784 as a 'halfway house' between company rule and crown rule is a recurring exam theme

concepts.name: Pitt's India Act and the Impeachment of Warren Hastings: Contextual Link
key_dimensions: Hastings' controversial actions (Rohilla War, Chait Singh affair, Begums of Oudh) created the political climate demanding the Act
Act strengthened oversight mechanisms precisely because Regulating Act had failed to prevent Hastings' excesses
Irony: Hastings was impeached in 1787 under laws strengthened by Pitt's Act, which he himself had partly shaped
UPSC trap: Pitt's Act did NOT directly cause the impeachment — it created the legal framework that enabled it

concepts.name: Pitt's Act in the Context of British Domestic Politics
key_dimensions: Act was William Pitt the Younger's solution to balance Crown authority, parliamentary accountability, and Company interests
Reflected Whig vs. Tory tensions over how much state control was appropriate over private enterprise
George III's role in defeating Fox's Bill and enabling Pitt's moderate alternative — royal prerogative vs. parliamentary power
Shows how Indian constitutional developments were deeply intertwined with British domestic political struggles

concepts.name: Limitations and Criticisms of Pitt's India Act
key_dimensions: Dual control created confusion and jurisdictional conflicts between Board and Directors — inefficiency in governance
No direct representation of Indian interests — purely a British administrative arrangement
Prohibition on wars was a dead letter — British territorial expansion accelerated after 1784
UPSC trap: Despite being celebrated as a landmark, the Act's practical limitations are equally examinable — balance both aspects
